title: How does electricity work in our body?
subtitle: Nerves & ions
subject: sciences
description: Thinking, beating of the heart, raising an arm: all this circulates first of all like living electricity, carried not by electrons, but by ions.

hero.hook: Your body is an electrical network. But here, the current is ions, not electrons.

blocks.text: In a wall socket, the current is **electrons** which circulate. In your body, it's different: they are **ions**, charged atoms, which enter and leave the cells. This flow creates the signals that make the heart think, the heart beat, and the muscle contract.
Without this living electricity, no thought, no gesture, no pulse. Understanding the body also means understanding this language of charges.

sections.title: The electric click of the neuron

blocks.text: A **neuron** at rest does not send a message, but it “charges”. Its membrane separates the inside and outside of the cell. Thanks to the , it maintains a  of approximately **-70 millivolts**: the inside is more negative than the outside. [[sodium-potassium pumps]] [[resting potential]]

blocks.caption: Neurons communicate through brief electrical impulses.

blocks.text: When a stimulus arrives, channels open. The sodium comes in all at once. The polarity is reversed: it is the , an all-or-nothing signal which runs along the axon, sometimes over a meter. Like an electric wave. [[The neuronal action potential]]
The waking brain produces about **20 watts**, enough for a small LED. However, it consumes almost **20%** of the body's calories.

sections.title: At the synapse, electricity becomes chemistry

blocks.text: The neurons don't really touch each other. Between them, a tiny gap: the **synapse**. The electrical signal cannot skip it. Then the end of the axon releases , messenger molecules such as acetylcholine or . [[Neurotransmitters]] [[glutamate]]
These messengers attach themselves to the next neuron like a key in a lock. Depending on the message, they excite or inhibit. Thousands of these simultaneous decisions form thought.
Some nerve signals travel at **120 m/s** (more than **430 km/h**). Enough to react to a burn on the toe in a split second.

sections.title: The heart has its own pacemaker

blocks.text: The heart does not wait for a command from the brain for each beat. In the right atrium, the **sinus node** generates its own impulses, approximately **60 to 100** times per minute at rest. The signal propagates, first contracts the atria, then the ventricles.

This activity is strong enough to be read on the skin: it is the **electrocardiogram (ECG)**. If the rhythm becomes disturbed, we speak of **arrhythmia**. The heart then beats disorderly and pumps poorly.
The electric eel uses the same principle of excitable cells, but in series: up to **600 volts**, enough to paralyze prey.
To raise the arm, an action potential travels down to the muscle. Acetylcholine triggers a local electrical wave, then a release of calcium. The muscle proteins slide over each other: contraction.

**defibrillation** uses the same principle in reverse: an external shock resets all the cells “to zero” so that the sinus node resumes tempo. Bionic prosthetics also capture these weak signals to control an artificial hand.
Living things speak in ion flows and action potentials. Thought, heart and muscles share the same electrical language.
